summary: Help 6–8 year olds name and USE habitat vocabulary (habitat, environment, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, woodland, ocean, desert, rainforest, pond) in context rather than reciting definitions. Two scales matter: the whole habitat (woodland, pond, desert) and the microhabitat nested inside it (under a log, a rock-pool crevice). Children justify why an animal suits a place using 'conditions', 'shelter' and 'adapted to'. Teach through describing real scenes and matching, and anchor 'microhabitat' to first-hand local exploration where possible.
misconceptions: Using 'habitat' to mean the animal's nest or home rather than the whole surrounding place.
Not grasping the microhabitat scale — treating 'under a log' as unrelated to the woodland it sits in.
Believing any animal can live in any habitat (ignoring conditions/suitability).
Confusing 'environment' and 'habitat' as identical, or using neither with precision.
Thinking only exotic places (jungle, desert) are habitats, not a local pond or hedge.

activities.title: Explore a labelled habitat scene and 'lift the log'
steps: Look at a cross-section countryside-to-coast picture holding woodland, pond, hedgerow and seashore.
Point to or tap each place, say its name, and state its conditions (a pond is wet; a wood is often shady and damp; a seashore is salty and windy; a hedgerow is sheltered and leafy).
Name one animal that lives in each place and say what it needs there (food, water, shelter, space).
'Lift the log' or zoom into a small damp, dark spot of woodlice and centipedes, and name it a microhabitat — a small habitat sitting inside the bigger woodland.
Compare the whole place (habitat) with one specific nest or burrow (shelter), saying aloud which word fits which.
activities.insight: A habitat is the whole place that supports many living things; a microhabitat is a smaller habitat nested within it; a shelter/nest is only the one spot where an animal hides. Each place has defining conditions that make it suit particular animals.

activities.title: Match animals to habitats and justify with conditions
steps: Match living-thing cards (animals and plants) to habitat scenes (cactus, a plant→desert; crab→rock pool; fox→woodland; frog→pond).
For each match, add a 'why?' using 'conditions', 'adapted to' or 'shelter' (e.g. 'a cactus is adapted to dry, sunny conditions').
Test a deliberately wrong pairing (cactus→pond) and explain why the conditions do not suit it.
Sort a second set of cards into 'whole habitat' vs 'microhabitat inside it'.
activities.insight: Not every living thing can live in any place; a match is justified by the conditions a place offers and what the plant or animal is adapted to. The habitat/microhabitat sort reinforces the two scales.

activities.title: Describe a habitat aloud using the target words
steps: Look at a rock pool or woodland picture.
Describe the place aloud: where a crab (or other animal) lives, what it is like there, and where it can hide.
Use whichever words fit while narrating: habitat, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, environment.

Answer follow-up prompts: point to a microhabitat inside the habitat; name the conditions that make a rock pool hard to live in; use 'environment' in a sentence about the seashore; decide whether a bird's nest is a habitat, a microhabitat or just a shelter, and why.
activities.insight: Meaning is shown by correct USE in running description — naming the whole place as the habitat/environment, a crevice as a microhabitat within it, the specific conditions (wet, salty, cold, pounding waves), and the animal's shelter — not by reciting definitions.

activities.title: Meet an animal who describes its home
steps: Listen to or read an animal persona describing where it lives and asking 'where do I live, and why does it suit me?'
Name the animal's habitat and the conditions it needs.
Point out a microhabitat within the habitat where the animal might find shelter, and say how the microhabitat and the shelter differ from the whole habitat.
activities.insight: The same vocabulary can be rehearsed through dialogue, prompting a child to supply habitat, conditions and shelter for a described animal.

checkQuestion: Show a picture of a rockpool at the seaside (or a woodland). Say: 'Describe this place to me — where a crab lives, what it is like there, and where it can hide. As you talk, use whichever of these words fit: habitat, microhabitat, conditions, shelter, environment.' Listen for how the words are used, not for definitions.
checkAnswer: Uses the terms accurately in running description: the rockpool/seashore is the habitat or environment; a crevice under a rock is a microhabitat within it; names the conditions (wet, salty, cold, pounding waves); identifies the crab's shelter (under a rock, in a crack). Meaning is shown by correct USE in context, not by reciting definitions.
